title: Rosenzweig's Not Yet
hookLine: asked whether he wore tefillin, Franz Rosenzweig is remembered answering "not yet"
carry: jewish law is built toward: not yet, not no
tomorrow: what if you started class from your life, not the book?

cards: Noa's application is due Friday. So far, one sentence. At dinner her mom asked if she's applying, and Noa said not yet, then wondered if she'd just said no.
Here's the difference. No closes a door. Not yet faces it.

The philosopher Franz Rosenzweig is remembered for exactly that answer. Someone asked if he put on tefillin, the leather straps and small black boxes worn at weekday morning prayer by Jews who keep the custom.
He didn't say no, and he didn't pretend. He said: not yet.

teach.b: Start with the object, because this is a lesson you can almost smell. Tefillin are leather: a box tied on the upper arm, its strap wound down toward the hand, and a second box worn at the top of the forehead.
The custom reads the Torah closely: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes."
People who wear them describe the snug pull of the strap and a faint mark on the arm that fades by breakfast. Rosenzweig hadn't taken that on.
But in an open letter called The Builders, he explained why not yet was an honest answer. He wrote that Jewish law isn't a fence you're either inside or outside.
It's a building, and each person builds toward it, taking up a practice when it becomes their own, when they can say this is mine.
Some readers hear in that a warning, too: not yet only works if you keep walking. It isn't a polite no.

teach.h: JEWISH LAW IS BUILT TOWARD: NOT YET, NOT NO.
teach.b: It's a direction with no deadline. That's the line worth telling a friend: the difference between no and not yet is which way you're facing.

how: Jews who keep the custom, traditionally men and in some communities women too, wear tefillin at weekday morning prayer, binding a leather box on the arm and one on the head; Rosenzweig's letter The Builders is read in discussions of how people take on practices over time.

o: a polite way of saying no to a request
a promise to do everything on a fixed date
a direction held open, not a refusal

games.q: a door held open — tap the pairs.
p: leather boxes and straps for morning prayer
bind them for a sign upon thy hand
Rosenzweig's letter on taking up the law

s: asked about tefillin, Rosenzweig is remembered answering no
Deuteronomy speaks of binding the words as a sign on the hand
and as frontlets between the eyes, the verse behind tefillin.
in The Builders, the law is all-or-nothing
he pictures each person building toward it, taking up what becomes their own.

games.q: your friend wants to start lighting Shabbat candles but says it feels fake, since she doesn't keep the rest of Shabbat. what would Rosenzweig's not yet say?
o: light them; take up one practice as it becomes yours, and keep building.
wait until she can keep all of Shabbat, or it doesn't count.
skip it; if she isn't all in, Jewish practice isn't for her.
games.why: Rosenzweig saw Jewish law as a building each person builds toward. one practice taken up honestly is a not yet, facing the door.

practice: Stand up, if you can. Name one thing you've been saying not yet to. Then take a slow minute of steps, around the room or down a hall, and with each step name one small piece of it: a page opened, a question asked, a first line.

wordCard.voice: Not yet: Franz Rosenzweig's remembered answer about tefillin. Not a refusal, but a direction, held open until the practice becomes your own.

carryVoice: Your line: Jewish law is built toward, not yet, not no. Rosenzweig's words face the door instead of closing it, as long as your feet keep moving.
